question: On 4 October 2024, the decision of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in joined cases [C-778/21P and C-798/21P] and [C-779/21P and C-799/21P] was announced.

The decision dismissed appeals lodged by the Commission and the Council against the judgments of the General Court (EU-T-2021-640 and EU-T-2021-639 respectively) concerning trade agreements between the European Union and the Kingdom of Morocco, particularly regarding fishery and agricultural products.

The decisions deemed the trade agreements null and void because, among other reasons, the Sahrawi people and their legitimate representatives, the Polisario Front, had not given their consent. The relevant legal consequences must follow the CJEU judgment, which upheld the General Court’s decision. In the light of these decisions: 1.
What measures will the Commission take to ensure that products originating in Western Sahara are not imported into the EU under the aforementioned agreements or agreements negotiated in the future?

What compensation will be provided for the damage caused by the illegal importing of products from Western Sahara in recent years under these two agreements, particularly as regards customs duties illegally not charged, among other issues?
Does the Commission intend to open talks with the Polisario Front, which the UN considers the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi people?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.1.2025) The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), in case C-779/21 P, has annulled the Council decision concluding the 2019 exchange of letters providing preferential tariffs to goods originating in Western Sahara.

However, the effects of this decision have been maintained by the Court for a period of twelve-months from 4 October 2024, the date of delivery of the judgment. Accordingly, the tariff preferences provided for under the EU-Morocco Agreement continue to be valid. During this period, products originating in Western Sahara continue to benefit from the effects of this agreement.

The judgement does not affect preferences already granted prior to the ruling. The Commission has taken note of the CJEU’s judgment in joined cases C-778/21P and C798/21P, and C-779/21 P and C-799/21P and is currently analysing it in detail. It is therefore too early to comment on any possible measure or talks following the CJEU’s ruling.
